answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

Art. 134 inciso final (maximum length of detention to carry out expulsion)

provisions.instrument: Constitución Política de la República de Chile

events.what_changed: Added a sentence saying the 48-hour limit for bringing detainees before a judge does not apply when an administrative expulsion is being carried out. Instead the law sets the maximum, which cannot exceed five calendar days. This concerns how long detention may last, not the right to challenge it; art. 21 amparo is untouched.
events.passage: Este lapso de cuarenta y ocho horas no se considerará para efectos de materialización de expulsiones administrativas. En este último caso, corresponderá a la ley fijar el plazo máximo, el que no podrá, en todo caso, exceder de cinco días corridos;

events.what_changed: Before: detention solely to carry out an expulsion was capped at 48 hours ('cuarenta y ocho horas'). After: the cap is five calendar days. A statutory length limit remains, so there is still a limit to enforce through amparo; the means of appeal did not change.
events.passage: En todo caso, el afectado podrá ser privado de libertad únicamente para hacer efectiva la expulsión por un plazo máximo de cincLey 21590 Art. único D.O. 07.08.2023o días corridos.

answers.implementation_then_now: In both periods, migrants held for expulsion used constitutional amparo before the Courts of Appeal and the Supreme Court, and courts granted it. In November 2023 orders not to proceed ('órdenes de no innovar') forced the PDI to release four Venezuelans awaiting a failed expulsion flight. In December 2025 the Supreme Court (Rol 51.745-2025) annulled an unreasoned PDI entry ban. The CPT (Chile's national torture-prevention mechanism) visited police facilities between November 2023 and October 2024. Its 2025 report found a lack of basic procedural guarantees in administrative detention for expulsion. That points to gaps in practice, but it is not a documented change from the earlier period. I see no shift; I keep the starting rating, though 'Usually' looks more accurate (see concern).

answers.starting_answer_concern: The protection answer holds: art. 21 of the Constitution reaches any unlawful arrest or detention and lets the court correct legal defects, and art. 95 of the Código Procesal Penal expressly covers legality and conditions. Length is covered through the statutory cap in art. 134 of Ley 21.325. The 'Effectively Always' rating has no evidence behind it. Known gaps argue for 'Usually': expulsions in 2021 went ahead before amparos were heard, and the 2025 CPT report found missing procedural guarantees.
answers.notes: Protection answer relies on statutes and the Constitution, not on a court ruling. The longer cap (48 h to 5 days) changes how long detention may lawfully last, not whether it can be challenged. Art. 141 of Ley 21.325 (judicial appeal against expulsion, with suspensive effect) is unchanged and supports the answer.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

events.what_changed: The maximum detention to carry out an expulsion rose from 48 hours to five calendar days. Detention is still allowed only once a specific person's expulsion order is final ('firme y ejecutoriada'), so the individualized basis is unchanged.
events.passage: Una vez que se encuentre firme y ejecutoriada la resolución que ordena la expulsión, se podrá someter al afectado a restricciones y privaciones de libertad. ... por un plazo máximo de cincLey 21590 Art. único D.O. 07.08.2023o días corridos.

events.what_changed: Immediate reconducción at the border, done without an expulsion order, used to cover only people caught trying to enter. It now also covers people who have already entered up to 10 km inside the border; identity must also be registered, and the provisional entry ban rose from six months to one year. This is a summary border return, not detention under art. 134. It widens removal without an individual expulsion decision, but it does not authorise detention without one.
events.passage: Asimismo, el extranjero que sea sorprendido por la autoridad contralora Ley 21655 Art. 2º a), b), c) y d) D.O. 20.02.2024intentando ingresar o habiendo ingresado al territorio nacional eludiendo el control migratorio ... o que se haya internado al territorio nacional hasta 10 kilómetros del límite fronterizo terrestre ... previa acreditación de su identidad y de su registro, será inmediatamente reembarcado o reconducido

answers.implementation_then_now: Detention for expulsion follows an individual expulsion resolution in both periods, and art. 130 (individual analysis, no collective expulsions) is unchanged. Courts kept reviewing individual cases. In 2023 amparos stopped expulsions and led to releases. In December 2025 the Supreme Court (Rol 51.745-2025) annulled a PDI entry ban for failing to weigh personal and family circumstances. That case is about entry bans, not detention, but it shows formulaic, non-individualized PDI action. The 2025 CPT report (visits November 2023–October 2024) also found gaps in procedural guarantees. Neither source shows a change from the earlier period, so I keep the starting rating.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'Yes' holds on art. 134 (detention only after a final individual expulsion order) read with art. 130 (each case analysed individually). Art. 133 is about revoking expulsion orders and adds little. The 'Effectively Always' rating is unsupported. Summary reconducciones under art. 131, widened in 2024, involve brief holding without an individual expulsion decision, and Supreme Court rulings find PDI measures that ignore personal circumstances. 'Usually' looks more defensible.
answers.notes: The protection answer relies on the statute, not on a ruling. Ley 21.655's change to reconducción is recorded because it extends removal without an individual expulsion resolution; I do not treat it as changing the answer, since art. 131 does not authorise detention.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 but they are not the same

provisions.instrument: Constitución Política de la República de Chile
provisions.article: Art. 19 Nº 1 ('Se prohíbe la aplicación de todo apremio ilegítimo')

events.article: Código Penal, art. 150 D, incisos primero y segundo
events.what_changed: Before, the crime of illegitimate coercion or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment covered any official who acted 'abusando de su cargo o sus funciones'. It also punished failure to stop it 'o estando en posición', and gave a higher penalty when the victim was in the official's custody. After, it covers an official who 'en incumplimiento de los reglamentos respectivos actúe abusando de su cargo o que en el ejercicio de sus funciones' inflicts it. Liability for failing to stop it now requires authority 'y estando en posición', and the custody aggravation is gone, which matters for detained migrants. The offence still exists, so the answer stays 'Yes', but the cited protection is narrower.
events.passage: 2. Reemplázanse los incisos primero y segundo del artículo 150 D, por los siguientes: "Artículo 150 D.- El empleado público que, en incumplimiento de los reglamentos respectivos actúe abusando de su cargo o que en el ejercicio de sus funciones, aplique, ordene o consienta en que se apliquen apremios ilegítimos u otros tratos crueles, inhumanos o degradantes, que no alcancen por su gravedad a constituir tortura

answers.implementation_then_now: No source I found shows systematic torture of migrants by Chilean authorities in either period. The CPT (Chile's national torture-prevention mechanism) visited police facilities holding migrants for expulsion between November 2023 and October 2024. Its 2025 report found material conditions and practices that may amount to a risk of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and a lack of basic guarantees. That is evidence of gaps in 2023–2025. I found no comparable monitoring for before 2023, and nothing that shows a change in practice, so I keep the starting rating. The evidence covers migrants detained for expulsion (mostly irregular), not migrants generally or asylum seekers.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'Yes' holds: art. 19 Nº 1 of the Constitution bans all illegitimate coercion for 'todas las personas'; arts. 150 A–D criminalise torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment regardless of nationality; and art. 3 of Ley 21.325 protects the human rights of foreigners 'sin importar su condición migratoria'. The rating 'Usually; Effectively Always' rests on no cited evidence. The CPT's 2023–2024 findings argue for 'Usually' at most for detained migrants.
answers.notes: The protection answer relies on the Constitution and statutes; treaties (CAT, Decree 808/1988) are cited only as background. I chose 'not the same' because art. 150 D, a cited provision, was narrowed in the window even though the option stays 'Yes'. A reviewer could reasonably treat the change as immaterial to the indicator and code 'no change'.
